_what_this_is: Google's documented required and recommended fields for the rich-result
features this tool checks. This is Google's publisher policy, NOT the
schema.org vocabulary: every rule here concerns markup that is already
vocabulary-valid. A property Google requires is one whose absence stops the
rich result appearing, not one schema.org objects to.
Hand-curated rather than generated. Google's documentation is prose with no
machine-readable form, so unlike data/schema-subclasses.json there is no
fetch script to regenerate this — see `source` on each type for the page it
came from, and `retrieved` above for when.
_entry: `entry: true` means the type is judged wherever it is found. `entry: false`
means it is judged ONLY when reached from an entry type along a `follow`
property, because that is how Google evaluates it: Offer's price requirement
belongs to the product snippet, not to every Offer node in existence. A
stray Offer nobody references is not a Google finding, and reporting one is
how this check would start inventing work.
_most_specific_wins: Rules are dispatched on a node's MOST SPECIFIC declared type, never on every
match in its class closure, and never on the property that reached it.
The corpus proved why. AggregateOffer is a subclass of Offer, so a closure
match hits both — and five corpus AggregateOffer nodes were reported as
missing Offer's required `price` when they correctly carry `lowPrice`
instead. All five were false positives. Same shape for AggregateRating
_dotted_paths: A field may be written `a.b`, satisfied when the node reached through `a`
carries `b`. Google uses this spelling for genuine alternatives, and the
corpus proved it is load-bearing: one Offer carries its price as
`priceSpecification.price`, which Google accepts and a rule knowing only
`price` reported as a missing required field. One level only.
_excluded: Recipe, JobPosting, HowTo, Course, Book and Movie have ZERO instances across
the 22-site corpus, so no rule for them could be shaken down. They are
absent deliberately: an unvalidated rule is how false positives ship.
Article/NewsArticle/BlogPosting are excluded although 850 nodes carry them
on 13 sites. Google's required set for Article is now nearly empty, and the
corpus is at 100% on headline, author and datePublished. The only gap is
`image` at 86%, which is nearer Screaming Frog's territory than ours.
Organization is excluded despite 2,204 nodes on 19 sites: it is sitewide
header markup, judging it per page floods the report, and
coverage.missing-expected-entity already covers logo and sameAs.

_note: priceCurrency is required for merchant listings and only recommended for
product snippets. The weaker reading is used deliberately: this tool
cannot tell which feature a site is going for, and over-claiming a
requirement is worse than under-claiming one.
These are Google's requirements for an Event's location, which is the
only position a bare Place is judged in. A LocalBusiness reached as a
location is judged by LocalBusiness's rules instead — it is the more
specific type, and its own entry applies.
review and aggregateRating are omitted from `recommended` on purpose.
Google recommends them only for sites that review OTHER businesses, and
flags self-serving reviews as ineligible — so prompting a business to
add reviews of itself would be advice to break the guidelines.
bestRating and worstRating are listed as recommended by Google and are
deliberately NOT checked. They default to 5 and 1, which is what a
five-star scale means anyway, so their absence is not a gap.
This was caught by the shakedown, not by review: the first version
reported both on 14 nodes of one corpus site, and the finding amounted
to telling an operator to declare that five is the best of five. The
test the corpus taught: a recommended field whose documented default
already says what the site means is redundant advice, and redundant
advice is what makes a report get ignored.
